entities.name: Five Pagoda Temple of Hohhot
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Five Pagoda Temple (Wuta Si) in Hohhot, Inner Mongolia, China, built in 1732 CE during the Qing dynasty's reign of the Yongzheng Emperor, is a unique architectural monument combining Indian-style vajra throne (diamond throne) design — a form originating in Buddhist India (the Bodh Gaya Mahabodhi Temple) — with Chinese architectural decoration, making it one of the finest examples of the synthesis between Tibetan-Mongolian Buddhism and Chinese imperial architecture.

The Five Pagoda Temple's most remarkable feature is its southern wall relief, which contains an astronomical chart inscribed in Mongolian script — one of only three known astronomical charts written in Mongolian, and a unique document of Mongolian scientific knowledge during the Qing period. The chart depicts the celestial sphere with constellation positions translated into the Mongolian astronomical tradition, making it invaluable for historians of Inner Asian science.

The Five Pagoda Temple was built under the auspices of the Qing dynasty's policy of patronizing Tibetan-Mongolian Buddhism as a means of consolidating control over Mongolia and Tibet: the Qing emperors (particularly Qianlong) built extensive Buddhist monuments throughout Inner Mongolia and Beijing's Tibetan-style temples (such as Yong He Gong) as tools of imperial soft power. The Hohhot temple's diamond-throne design, modeled on Indian prototypes, represents the meeting point of Indian Buddhist theology, Tibetan religious art, Mongolian culture, and Chinese imperial architecture in a single building.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Five Pagoda Temple of Hohhot — synthesizing Indian Buddhist, Tibetan, Mongolian, and Chinese architectural traditions, preserving one of only three known Mongolian astronomical charts, and embodying the Qing dynasty's Buddhist soft-power policy in Inner Mongolia — is a unique document of cultural synthesis at the intersection of four civilizations.
